sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: City A's high temperatures (°F) for 5 days were 68, 70, 72, 74, 76. City B's high temperatures for 5 days were 60, 70, 72, 74, 90. Which measure of center is the same for both cities?
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. Median A = 72 (middle of 68,70,72,74,76). Median B = 72 (middle of 60,70,72,74,90) -- equal. Mean A=72 but Mean B=73.2 -- different. Neither set has a repeated value, so there's no mode.
questions.explanation: Median A = 72 (middle of 68,70,72,74,76). Median B = 72 (middle of 60,70,72,74,90) -- equal. Mean A=72 but Mean B=73.2 -- different. Neither set has a repeated value, so there's no mode.

questions.q: Consider a survey of 800 randomly selected voters found that 66% support a new public transit initiative, with an associated margin of error of 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. Which of the following is the most plausible conclusion from this result?
questions.answer:
**Answer:** D. A sample estimate with a margin of error \(\pm m\) creates a confidence interval \([p - m, p + m]\) for the true population parameter.
Here, the interval is \([66 - 3\%, 66 + 3\%] = [63\%, 69\%]\).
This interval represents plausible values for the actual percentage of the entire target population, not just the sample.
questions.explanation:
A sample estimate with a margin of error \(\pm m\) creates a confidence interval \([p - m, p + m]\) for the true population parameter.
Here, the interval is \([66 - 3\%, 66 + 3\%] = [63\%, 69\%]\).
This interval represents plausible values for the actual percentage of the entire target population, not just the sample.
choices: If another survey of 800 voters is conducted, exactly 66% of them will support the initiative.
Exactly 66% of all voters in the population definitely support the initiative.
Between 60% and 72% of the sample respondents supported the initiative.
It is plausible that the true proportion of voters in the entire population who support the initiative is between 63% and 69%.

questions.answer:

Here, the interval is \([59 - 4\%, 59 + 4\%] = [55\%, 63\%]\).
This interval represents plausible values for the actual percentage of the entire target population, not just the sample.

Here, the interval is \([59 - 4\%, 59 + 4\%] = [55\%, 63\%]\).

questions.q: Using the same monthly phone-sales table (Jan through Dec: 100, 105, 110, 130, 150, 180, 170, 160, 140, 120, 115, 110), what is the average monthly increase in phones sold from January to December?
questions.answer: **Answer:** B. Net change from Jan to Dec \( =110-100=10 \), over 11 monthly intervals: \( 10/11\approx0.9 \) phones/month.
questions.explanation: Net change from Jan to Dec \( =110-100=10 \), over 11 monthly intervals: \( 10/11\approx0.9 \) phones/month.

questions.q: The bar graph shows the results of rolling a fair die 40 times. Based on the experimental data, find the experimental probability of rolling a 4, and compare it to the theoretical probability.
questions.answer: Experimental \(P(4)=\frac{9}{40}=0.225\). Theoretical \(P(4)=\frac{1}{6}\approx0.167\). The experimental probability is somewhat higher than the theoretical probability, which is expected random variation in a finite sample.
questions.explanation: Experimental \(P(4)=\frac{9}{40}=0.225\). Theoretical \(P(4)=\frac{1}{6}\approx0.167\). The experimental probability is somewhat higher than the theoretical probability, which is expected random variation in a finite sample.

questions.q: A game costs 2 dollars to play. A player wins 10 dollars with probability 0.1, and wins nothing otherwise. Find the expected net profit per play.
questions.answer: Expected winnings \(=0.1\times10=1\) dollar. Expected net profit \(=1-2=-1\) dollar (an expected loss of 1 dollar per play).
questions.explanation: Expected winnings \(=0.1\times10=1\) dollar. Expected net profit \(=1-2=-1\) dollar (an expected loss of 1 dollar per play).

This question has three parts. A researcher surveys 200 students about whether they play a sport and whether they play a musical instrument. Of the 200 students, 120 play a sport, 80 play an instrument, and 30 do both. (a) Find how many students do neither activity. (b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen student plays a sport or an instrument (or both). (c) Given that a randomly selected student plays a sport, find the probability that they also play an instrument.
questions.target: A well-designed word problem: a survey of students
questions.answer: (a) By inclusion-exclusion, the number doing at least one activity is \(120+80-30=170\). Neither \(=200-170=30\). (b) \(P(\mathrm{sport\ or\ instrument})=\frac{170}{200}=0.85\). (c) \(P(\mathrm{instrument}\mid\mathrm{sport})=\frac{P(\mathrm{both})}{P(\mathrm{sport})}=\frac{30}{120}=\frac{1}{4}\).
questions.explanation: (a) By inclusion-exclusion, the number doing at least one activity is \(120+80-30=170\). Neither \(=200-170=30\). (b) \(P(\mathrm{sport\ or\ instrument})=\frac{170}{200}=0.85\). (c) \(P(\mathrm{instrument}\mid\mathrm{sport})=\frac{P(\mathrm{both})}{P(\mathrm{sport})}=\frac{30}{120}=\frac{1}{4}\).
